With this definition of "improper governmental activity," concerns raised earlier by groups such as the California County Counsels Association and the California Association of Sanitation Agencies have been addressed. However, the Attorney General is still concerned about the potential harmful effect of allowing disclosure of what would otherwise be privileged information between attorney and client under the aegis of "improper governmental activity." The definition of the phrase (which earlier included phrases drawn from Rule 3-600, such as "a violation of law reasonably imputable to the organization"), the Attorney General argues, leaves the interpretation of what is improper governmental activity to the individual attorney and his or her personal and political views. "While we may all agree that certain conduct, such as the Quackenbush mis-administration (sic) of the Department of Insurance, should see the light of day, we may have legitimate differences of opinion about whether a governmental activity is "likely to result in substantial injury to the organization," involves "willful misuse of public funds" or "breach of fiduciary duty," or involves the "willful omission to perform" an official duty. The proposed exceptions?will unwisely empower attorneys representing public agencies to act as free agents subject to their personal viewpoint, and place them in a state of perpetual conflict with their clients, chilling the trust and open access to information essential to their profession and compromising their effectiveness." [Letter from the Attorney General's Office, dated June 27, 2002.] The Attorney General suggests limiting the definition of "improper governmental activity" to "conduct that constitutes or would constitute a felony." With this definition, the AG states, there would be little difference between attorneys in interpretation of conduct that should clearly be reported. The Attorney General makes a good point. A broad definition might embolden publicity-seeking disclosures by loose cannons, to the detriment of the government agency. However, their suggested amendment may narrow the bill too much. For example, it is not clear if an agency official who used a government charge card to purchase a personal item during official travel is guilty of a felony. A possible consequence of that narrow amendment is a spate of future legislative measures to upgrade current misdemeanors to felonies, just to protect the government attorney whistleblower. There are other phrases used in the Government Code that also may be used to limit these exceptions to the attorney-client confidentiality rule, such as conduct that is "willful or corrupt misconduct in office" that would be grounds for removal of a public official from office. [Government Code Section 3060 et seq.] This phrase has been extensively interpreted in case law to apply to situations that would appear to be "improper governmental activity" as defined by , although the situations are limited to local agency officials, including school district officials. has been amended to remove from the definition of "improper governmental activity" undefined violations of law "reasonably imputable to the organization" or "likely to cause substantial injury to the organization," which, under Rule 3-600, could trigger an attorney representing an organization to take actions consistent with Section 6068(e) or, if necessary, resign. Thus "improper government activity" includes conduct that is less definitive than a felony, as the Attorney General would prefer, but would fall under "willful or corrupt misconduct in office," "willful or breach of fiduciary duty," "willful misuse of public funds," and conduct constituting "crime, fraud, or serious and willful violations of law." In all of the above cases, the improper governmental activity should probably be tied to substantial harm to the public interest, so that the attorney would be compelled to take the protected actions in order to prevent or rectify the improper governmental activity. First order of action: urge reconsideration and/or go to highest internal authority Under this bill, an attorney who learns of improper governmental activity in the course of representing a governmental organization may take one or both actions specified by Rule 3-600 (B)(1) [urge reconsideration of the matter while explaining its likely consequences to the organization] and (2) [refer the matter to the highest internal authority if warranted]. These actions would be subject to the Section 6068(e) rule of confidentiality, as they are under current law. By specifying the actions that an attorney may take when he or she learns of improper governmental activity, establishes a clear path of action for the attorney to take, rather than a broad spectrum of undefined actions that could be proper under Rule 3-600 (those actions that are "in the best, lawful interest of the organization"). Anthem Blue Cross (Anthem) states that this bill sets up an Exchange framework that is inconsistent with the concept of consumer choice by requiring the exchange to "determine health benefits." Furthermore, Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes benefit tiers and "essential health benefits" for the individual and small employer markets, whether coverage is purchased inside or outside the Exchange, and that having the Exchange "determine and approve benefit designs" is duplicative of federal requirements and will only serve to further limit consumer choice. Anthem writes that this bill makes the Exchange an "active purchaser," thus allowing it to set prices. Anthem states that the PPACA already establishes a rate review process for premiums charged in the individual and small group markets, which will be executed by the CDI and DMHC. Anthem states that if both the regulators and the Exchange are responsible for approving rates without a consistent process, the rates for the same product could be different inside and outside of the Exchange, violating the federal requirement that the entire market be treated as a single risk pool. Finally, Anthem asserts that setting rates in the Exchange would likely politicize the rate- setting process, which has proven to lead to insurer insolvency and insurers withdrawing from the market, reducing choices for consumers. Anthem suggests amending this bill to remove these provisions and instead clarifying that regulation of health plan and insurance products sold through the exchange are the sole purview of the CDI and DMHC. The Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies (ACLHIC) writes that the Exchange appears to have the power to negotiate rates for the products sold within the Exchange, and at the same time, requires participating carriers to offer the same products outside the Exchange. ACLHIC is concerned that these negotiated rates may not be actuarially sound and place participating carriers at a market disadvantage with nonparticipating carriers. ACLHIC states that participating carriers should compete on quality and price. ACLHIC also writes that there is already extensive criteria for carrier certification to participate in an Exchange included in PPACA, and will be further expanded when federal rules come forward, and that additional and potentially conflicting state standards may serve to limit the choice of plan in the Exchange. ACLHIC argues that, given the robust certification criteria that will already apply, any carrier that can meet those criteria should be eligible to participate in the Exchange. The California Hospital Association (CHA) is concerned over the provision in this bill that specifically expand the role of County Organized Health Systems beyond the original scope and purpose. Compline provides this information in a user-friendly, electronic format on a subscription basis to hundreds of insurance agents and brokers in California. As existing law does not provide for information service companies to have direct access to ex-mod information gathered by the WCIRB, Compline's current source of ex-mod information is through admitted workers' compensation insurers. These insurers are statutorily required to share information on their policyholders with the WCIRB, and, in turn, they can access, in hard copy, WCIRB's consolidated statewide data concerning employer ex-mods and related information. The sponsors state that this bill is necessary in light of plans by the WCIRB to institute a new, on-line system that will allow the WCIRB to provide information, including ex-mod information, electronically to member insurers and agents and brokers who subscribe to the system. This new system is very similar to the system that information service companies currently have in place. The sponsors argue that unless information service companies, such as Compline, can obtain the same information, in the same format and at the same time as the WCIRB intends to release it, information service companies will be unable to compete. The result, sponsors contend, will be that the WCIRB, a quasi-public entity created to collect, compile and analyze data required to be submitted to it from every admitted workers' compensation insurer, will be the exclusive provider of ex-mod information and other related information. The sponsors assert that establishing the WCIRB as the sole provider of this information was not the Legislature's intent, nor was it their intent to allow the WCIRB to develop an exclusive for-profit franchise to sell information to workers' compensation insurance agents and brokers. The sponsors argue that this bill will maintain a competitive market in the business of providing access to workers' compensation ex-mod and other related information, which is used by insurance agents and brokers to facilitate the placement of workers' compensation insurance on behalf of their clients. Without this legislation, the sponsors assert that competition in providing access to this information will be drastically reduced or eliminated
